questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication proves who the caller is; authorization decides what that caller may do
They are two names for the same check
Authorization happens first, then authentication
Authentication is only for humans, authorization only for services
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity (password, token, certificate). Authorization then checks permissions for that identity on the requested action or resource.

questions.prompt: Which header usually carries an OAuth 2.0 access token to an API?
options: Authorization: Bearer <token>
Cookie: token=<token>
X-Token-Type: OAuth
Accept: Bearer
questions.explanation: RFC 6750 defines the Bearer scheme in the Authorization header. Cookies can carry sessions but are not the standard for bearer tokens; the other headers do not exist for this purpose.

questions.prompt: An API key identifies the calling application, but on its own it does not identify which end user is acting.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: API keys are usually per application or per client. To know the end user you need user authentication such as OAuth tokens or sessions.

questions.prompt: A JWT payload decodes to this JSON. The current Unix time is 1767225600. What should a correctly configured API do?
options: Reject it with 401 because the token has expired
Accept it because the signature is valid
Return 403 because the role is wrong
Accept it because iat is in the past
questions.explanation: `exp` (1767222000) is before now (1767225600), so the token expired an hour ago and must be rejected as unauthenticated (401). A valid signature does not override expiry; `iat` being in the past is normal.

questions.prompt: Which authorization tests belong in a suite for GET /accounts/{id}? Select all that apply.
options: Owner reads own account: 200
Another normal user reads it: 403 or 404, no data
Support role reads it, if the policy allows: 200
No token: 401
Owner reads it twice: 200 both times
questions.explanation: A role/ownership matrix covers owner, other user, privileged role and anonymous. Repeating the same owner call twice is not an authorization case.

questions.prompt: After a user logs out, their old access token still works for 50 more minutes. Is this a defect?
options: It depends on the design: stateless JWTs stay valid until exp unless the API checks revocation; flag it if the requirements say logout must end access immediately
Always a critical defect in every design
Never a defect
Only a defect if the token is an API key
questions.explanation: Self-contained JWTs are usually not revoked on logout; mitigation is short lifetimes plus refresh-token revocation or a deny-list. Testers compare behaviour with the stated requirement and report the risk clearly.

questions.prompt: A token issued for `aud: reporting-api` is accepted by the payments API. What is the risk and the right test?
options: The payments API is not validating the audience, so tokens for other services can be replayed against it; test that a wrong-aud token gets 401
No risk because the signature is valid
The token needs a longer expiry
It is a CORS issue
questions.explanation: Audience validation ensures a token is used only for the API it was issued to. Without it, any service holding a token for another API could call payments.

questions.prompt: This lab test for role checks passes even though normal users can delete products. Why?
questions.code:
user_token = login('admin@example.test')  # copied from another test
r = delete('/products/5', token=user_token)
assert r.status_code == 204
options: The token used is the admin's, so the test never exercises the normal-user path
DELETE should return 200
The assertion should be `!= 204`
Bearer tokens cannot be used on DELETE
questions.explanation: The variable name says user but it holds the admin token, so the 204 is correct for that caller. Build tokens from clearly separated fixtures per role and assert 403 for the normal user.

coding.title: Check JWT claims
coding.prompt:
Write `check_claims(claims, now, audience)` returning a list of problems for a decoded JWT payload dict (assume the signature was already verified). Return, in this order where they apply: `'expired'` if `exp` is missing or `exp <= now`; `'not yet valid'` if `nbf` is present and `nbf > now`; `'wrong audience'` if `aud` (a string or a list of strings) does not contain `audience`.

Example: `check_claims({'exp': 200, 'aud': 'api'}, 100, 'api')` returns `[]`.
coding.explanation: These are the standard registered-claim checks from RFC 7519 that an API must apply after verifying the signature. `aud` can be a single string or an array, so normalise it to a list.
hints: Use `claims.get(...)` so missing claims do not crash.
A missing exp should be treated as invalid for access tokens here.
Wrap a string `aud` in a list before checking membership.

coding.title: Authorization matrix from a policy
coding.prompt:
Write `expected_status(role, action, is_owner)` for this policy and use it to drive parametrised tests:

- `anonymous` -> always `401`
- `admin` -> `200` for any action
- `user` -> `read`/`update` allowed (`200`) only on own resources; `delete` never allowed. Not allowed -> `403`.
- any other role -> `403`

Example: `expected_status('user', 'update', False)` returns `403`.
coding.explanation: Encoding the policy as an oracle lets you generate every role x action x ownership combination as a test case, so none are forgotten. Unknown roles fall through to deny-by-default.
hints: The only allowed user combination needs all three conditions.

tests.name: Anonymous and admin
tests.code:
assert expected_status('anonymous', 'read', True) == 401
assert expected_status('admin', 'delete', False) == 200

tests.name: User ownership rules
tests.code:
assert expected_status('user', 'read', True) == 200
assert expected_status('user', 'update', False) == 403
assert expected_status('user', 'delete', True) == 403
